title_he: אִם־בָּא שָׂשׂוֹן לַלֵּב, קוּמוּ הוֹדוּ וְזַמְּרוּ
review: 4:4 וְהָרוּחַ מַפְגִּיעַ בָּנוּ — Rom 8:26 (וְהָרוּחַ בְּעַצְמוֹ מַפְגִּיעַ בַּעֲדֵנוּ); the Arabic وَالرُّوحُ فِينَا يَشْفَعُ is that intercession, and מַפְגִּיעַ is the glossary term for the Spirit's pleading, kept so the line stays that verse and not a generic 'helps'.

2:2–2:4 תַּנְחוּמוֹת הָרוּחַ … קוֹל קוֹרְאוֹ הֶעָצוּב — the Arabic تَعْزِيَةَ الرُّوحِ الْأَمِينِ … صَوْتِ دَاعِيهِ الْحَزِين is 'the faithful Spirit's comfort … His grieving caller's voice'; the Hebrew keeps the voice as the thing heard across 2:4, so the Father's non-forgetfulness lands on the cry.

3:4 יַמְתִּיק הַלְּבָבוֹת — the Arabic يُطَيِّبُ الْقُلُوب is 'sweetens the hearts'; הִמְתִּיק is the biblical verb (Ps 119:103 אִמְרָתְךָ … מַמְתִּיק לְחִכִּי), so the comfort is tasted as in hymn 172.

1:2–1:3 קוּמוּ הוֹדוּ … רוֹמְמוּ — the imperative chain of the Arabic (قُومُوا احْمَدُوا وَرَنِّمُوا) is kept as three imperatives, with הוֹדוּ as the root of 'thanks' and זַמְּרוּ the song, so the summons stays three-fold.
2:1 בָּעֶצֶב — 'in grief'; עֶצֶב is the biblical noun of toil/sorrow (Gen 3:16, Prov 14:13), kept over the Modern Hebrew צַעַר, so the line pairs grief with prayer the way the psalmist does.
